gallery.filename: Multi-use trail open, levee path closed during construction (7728865214).jpg
gallery.title: File:Multi-use trail open, levee path closed during construction (7728865214).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: Contractors for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District haul away levee material Aug. 2, 2012, during the Howe Avenue levee raise project’s early stages. The top of the levee is closed to the public but fencing surrounds the project area, keeping the 33-mile multi-use trail (right) open to the public. After scheduled completion this October, the project will further reduce area flood risk by raising and reinforcing more than 4,000 feet of levee along the American River in Sacramento, Calif. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

gallery.title: File:Beavers sample American River habitat (6643655459).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: Recently uprooted almond trees intended for American River habitat, shown Jan. 4, 2012, demonstrate wear and tear from beavers between the Watt Avenue boat launch and Mayhew Drain in Sacramento, Calif. The metal fence (foreground) will serve as a barrier to protect a total of 6,785 plants at two erosion repair sites from the beavers, until the plants can sustain themselves.The plants were placed more than 15 feet away from the levee to comply with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers safety standards for vegetation on levees, improving river habitat without compromising levee stability. It’s all part of the Sacramento River Bank Protection Project, a joint effort between the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District and Central Valley Flood Protection Board to reduce flood risk by maintaining levees and reducing stream bank erosion along the Sacramento River and its tributaries. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

gallery.title: File:CBS Sacramento’s Morning Show (6313334568).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District project manager Dave Cook (right) participates in an interview with CBS Sacramento’s Morning Show to explain why two critical erosion sites are under repair along the American River’s south bank, Nov. 1, 2011. Cook is overseeing repairs of the sites, part of the Sacramento River Bank Protection Project to repair erosion, levees and reduce flood risk for Sacramento. (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Photo / Tyler Stalker)

gallery.filename: Folsom Dam on the American River (5384724149).jpg
gallery.title: File:Folsom Dam on the American River (5384724149).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: FOLSOM, Calif. (Jan. 24, 2011) - Looking west and downstream in an aerial view over Folsom Dam on the American River, prior to construction of the Folsom Lake Crossing bridge here on March 16, 2004. The U. S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District was authorized to build the bridge in 2004, after security concerns closed the road atop the dam, a major commuter throughway, in 2003. The Corps completed the bridge in March 2009.

gallery.filename: Winter water releases at the Folsom Spillway (5320592488).jpg
gallery.title: File:Winter water releases at the Folsom Spillway (5320592488).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: FOLSOM, Calif. (Jan. 4, 2011) - Water continues to be released at the Folsom Dam here Dec. 30. Flows were rated at about 13,000 cubic feet per second (cfs), down from the over 30,000 cfs that was being released Dec. 16. A retaining wall keeps the flow directed into the American River and out of the construction site for the new spillway and access roadway.

gallery.title: File:Folsom Dam Water Release (5268527059).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: FOLSOM, Calif. (Dec. 17, 2010) - Water releases from Folsom Dam into the American River reached 30,000 cubic feet per second here Dec. 16. The releases were made as a precautionary measure to increase storage capacity in the lake with the impending heavy rainstorms due to arrive here in the next few days.

gallery.title: File:Folsom Dam Spillway construction (5263755594).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: FOLSOM, Calif. (Dec.14, 2010) – Construction continues on an auxiliary spillway for Folsom Dam here Dec. 7. The spillway will allow for more manageable water releases from Folsom Lake to the lower American River, substantially reducing the risk of catastrophic flooding in the Sacramento metropolitan area.

gallery.title: File:Corps judges STEM-inspired student regatta (17947444439).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District engineers Zeffy Ruvalcaba and Josh Wagner helped judge 51 middle and high school teams competing in Folsom High School's eighth annual Cardboard/Plywood/Whatever Regatta at Lake Natoma in Folsom, California, May 22, 2015. Shown are the winners for best in design and construction. The event is led by Folsom High's physics teacher Eric Wright, who says the competition is a great way for students to apply their science, technology, engineering and math (or STEM) skills in a fun and interesting way. Competition categories include best in design and construction, using most recycled materials, fastest and slowest boats. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

gallery.filename: Corps contractor tags one of 6,785 total plants (6643664269).jpg
gallery.title: File:Corps contractor tags one of 6,785 total plants (6643664269).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: A U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contractor tags one of the 3,696 plants, comprised of 14 native species, being planted and cared for during the final phase of river-bank erosion repairs along the American River’s south bank in Sacramento, Calif., Jan. 4, 2012. A total of 6,785 plants at two erosion sites within one-half mile of each other will be nourished for at least three years by a river-water irrigation system, while a waist-high fence will guard against beavers and other animal populations until the plants can sustain themselves.The plants were placed more than 15 feet away from the levee to comply with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers safety standards for vegetation on levees, improving river habitat without compromising levee stability. It’s all part of the Sacramento River Bank Protection Project, a joint effort between the Corps’ Sacramento District and Central Valley Flood Protection Board to reduce flood risk by maintaining levees and reducing stream bank erosion along the Sacramento River and its tributaries. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

gallery.filename: Corps contractor digs deep for answers (6462041219).jpg
gallery.title: File:Corps contractor digs deep for answers (6462041219).jpg
gallery.artist: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District
gallery.description: URS Corporation project engineer Pablo Naranjo holds up an empty soil sample tube along the American River’s north bank in Sacramento, Calif., Nov. 18, 2011. Engineers are assessing erosion and seepage risk along the riverbank as part of the Corps’ American River Common Features General Reevaluation Report, determining the federal plan to provide additional flood risk reduction to Natomas as well as the rest of the City and County of Sacramento. Digging between 50-90 feet deep, engineers are using the 24-inch-tall, 4-inch-wide tubes to capture sub-surface samples before sealing them with wax and sending them to a lab for analysis. The sampling areas are left in better condition than before: They are filled with special material that prevents water seepage. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)
